tldr: We built RoboARC, a benchmark of physical puzzles with tight geometric constraints such as millimeter-thin gaps, and evaluated state-of-the-art coding agents and VLA models. In a privileged regime with full simulator state and resets, the strongest agent solved 86% of the tasks. However, this dropped to 43% in a standard regime with only real-sensor inputs, and zero-shot VLA models could not solve a single puzzle.

overview:
Tasks like untangling cables, inserting a plate through a narrow slit, or separating interlocked puzzle pieces succeed only along a tiny set of geometrically viable motions. While traditional robotics benchmarks focus on large object counts or long horizons, they do not adequately measure the ability to reason out geometric constraints themselves.

To address this, the authors introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 physical puzzles defined by tight spatial constraints. Spanning six constraint types across rigid and soft materials on three robots, it features two evaluation setups: a Privileged regime where agents can read simulator states and reset freely, and a Standard regime where agents get only real-sensor inputs (RGB-D images and proprioception) in a single attempt without resets.

Evaluating seven LLM-based coding agents and four public Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models revealed that the top coding agent (GPT-6 Astra) achieved an 86% success rate in the Privileged regime, which dropped to 43% in the Standard regime. Zero-shot VLA models failed completely across 18 one-arm puzzles (0% success rate). A breakdown of failure modes shows that while agents estimate object positions down to the millimeter, they struggle to infer detailed part geometry. Only when both position and geometry are available together can agents reliably deduce the right motions.
contributions: Building RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 challenging manipulation tasks governed by tight geometric constraints and contact physics
Quantifying bottlenecks by contrasting a Privileged regime (full simulator state and resets) against a Standard regime (real-sensor inputs, single attempt)
Conducting comprehensive zero-shot evaluations across seven state-of-the-art coding agents and four VLA models
Uncovering a powerful synergy between knowing part geometry and object pose through fine-grained failure trajectory analysis

sections.heading: Why have robots solve physical puzzles now?
sections.summary: Tasks involving millimeter gaps cannot rely on transferring pre-collected demonstrations or skills. They demand on-the-spot motion reasoning tailored to local geometry. This section describes the motivation, core principles, and key findings of RoboARC, a benchmark focused on spatial constraints.
sections.details:
Many hard manipulation tasks in the real world come down to spatial constraints that satisfy only a few motions. Examples include passing a plate through a narrow slit, untying tangled cords, or separating interlocked puzzle pieces. Because viable motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, robots cannot solve them by merely imitating human demonstrations gathered elsewhere. In other words, they must look at the geometry and reason out the right motions on the fly.

However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on visual diversity or multi-step horizon length, overlooking the ability to clear geometric contact constraints. This paper introduces RoboARC, which can be thought of as a physical manipulation counterpart to the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC). It features three key characteristics:

- **Difficulty driven by geometric constraints**: 90 tasks across six constraint types spanning rigid and soft materials, demanding reasoning rather than imitation.
- **Two evaluation regimes**: A Privileged regime with full simulator state access and resets, alongside a Standard regime restricted to camera images and proprioception in a single attempt, isolating perceptual and planning bottlenecks.
- **Open to all policy types**: Evaluates both code-generating agents and vision-to-action VLA models under the exact same physics-based grader.

The results show that while the strongest agent (GPT-6 Astra) solved 86% of tasks in the Privileged regime, performance dropped to 43% in the Standard regime. Zero-shot VLA models solved 0 out of 18 tasks (0%). The study reveals that agents can only deduce the correct motions once they have a grasp of both geometry and pose.

sections.heading: How does it differ from existing benchmarks and policies?
sections.summary: This section surveys existing robotic manipulation literature and reasoning benchmarks to contextualize RoboARC's unique focus. The fundamental difference lies in targeting motion planning and control under strict geometric constraints and contact physics rather than task horizon length.
sections.details:
This section organizes related research into three main areas:

### Manipulation benchmarks and policies
Many benchmarks exist to evaluate VLA models and imitation learning. However, most base their difficulty on visual diversity or long horizons in everyday settings, like room tidying. While some explore furniture assembly or deformable manipulation, they typically evaluate skills in isolation. RoboARC focuses squarely on threading through the narrow passages left by spatial constraints.

### Spatial reasoning and physical puzzles
In classical motion planning, puzzles like the Alpha Puzzle served as premier test cases, but they assumed exact geometry was known beforehand. Recent reasoning benchmarks test puzzles on 2D images or abstract grids without evaluating physical contact and motion execution. RoboARC grades whether a robot can actually carry out contact-rich motions through to completion.

### Coding agents in robotics
Using LLMs to write code for robot control is growing rapidly, but existing benchmarks mostly focus on long-horizon household chores. RoboARC evaluates agents across both full-simulator access and real-sensor regimes, precisely pinpointing where coding agents stumble during geometric reasoning.

sections.heading: Benchmark design: 90 puzzles across two evaluation regimes
sections.summary: This section details RoboARC's formulation, task types, simulation environments, and strict quality control pipeline. Every task comes with a physics-based automatic grader and a verified reference solution.
sections.details:
Each RoboARC task consists of a frozen simulation scene, a robot, a natural language instruction, and a grader based on physical simulation states.

### 3.1 Problem formulation
Each task is modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The state $s$ includes joint angles, rigid body poses, deformable body shapes, and contact states. The fundamental difficulty is that viable state trajectories reaching the goal set $G$ lie within an extremely narrow tube formed around millimeter-scale gaps and knots. A minor error in geometric estimation causes the system to drop into regions with no solution.

### 3.2 Task composition and simulation
The suite contains 90 tasks across six constraint types (three rigid, three soft), comprising 78 puzzles across 19 families plus 12 IKEA furniture assembly tasks.
- **Rigid bodies**: Interlocking, narrow passage, assembly
- **Soft bodies**: Untangling, threading, shape control (such as spreading cloth)

The benchmark uses MuJoCo 3.14 with the bimanual ALOHA 2 and the Franka Panda. Agents receive up to 190 minutes (around 3 hours) of runtime per task.

### 3.3 Two observation regimes
- **Privileged regime**: Runs inside a container where agents have full access to simulator states and can reset to any point at will. Agents can plan motions through trial and error.
- **Standard regime**: Runs in an isolated container where agents receive only RGB-D camera streams (four viewpoints including wrist cameras) and proprioception. It is a single-attempt trial without resets, mirroring real hardware conditions.

### 3.4 Rigorous verification pipeline
Every task includes a human- or oracle-crafted reference solution verified to pass the grader. Furthermore, 46,662 stress-test runs were conducted to monitor penetration depths and eliminate physics engine glitches or false-positive pass-throughs.

sections.heading: Benchmarking frontier agents against VLA models
sections.summary: We evaluated seven coding agents and four public VLA models. While commercial coding agents solved 73% to 86% in the Privileged regime, scores dropped heavily in the Standard regime. Zero-shot VLA models had a 0% success rate.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental setup
Two categories of systems were evaluated:
- **Coding agents (7)**: Four commercial models (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon) and three open-weight models (Kimi 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash), each tested in specialized harness environments.
- **VLA models (4)**: Public models fine-tuned on the DROID dataset ($\pi_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, GR00T N1.7, Cosmos3-Nano-Policy), evaluated zero-shot across 18 corresponding single-arm Franka puzzles.

### 4.2 Main results
- **Commercial agents dominate in the Privileged regime**: The four commercial agents solved 73% to 86% of the tasks, led by GPT-6 Astra at 86%. Open-weight models peaked at 31%.
- **Success rates halve in the Standard regime**: With only real-sensor inputs, GPT-6 Astra dropped to 43%, and other commercial models fell between 29% and 36%. Assembly and threading proved especially brutal, with no agent clearing 10% in assembly. Open-weight models topped out at 7%.
- **VLA models fail completely (0% success rate)**: While VLA models touched target objects in 31% to 61% of trials, they failed to solve a single puzzle across 216 runs (0 wins). Current imitation-based end-to-end policies cannot handle these geometric constraints zero-shot.

### 4.3 Real-robot transfer experiment
Using the Standard regime interface, we tested robots on a physical buzz wire game with a YAM arm and RealSense cameras. Comparing GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 (first and second place in simulation), GPT-6 Astra consistently navigated the loop farther along the wire, achieving 100% progress in later runs. This confirmed that simulation rankings correlate well with real-world execution.

captions.F6: Real-robot buzz wire experiment results. GPT-6 Astra (top, blue) navigated the ring farther along the wire more consistently than Claude Opus 5.5 (middle, red), matching their ranking in the simulated Standard regime.

sections.heading: Why do they fail? Error analysis and agent strategies
sections.summary: To find why performance drops in the Standard regime, we ran ablation experiments adding privileged information back incrementally and analyzed over 2,200 failure logs. This revealed strong synergies between pose and geometry, as well as common planning and execution bottlenecks.
sections.details:
### 5.1 The synergy between pose and geometry
Using 15 rigid-body puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime but failed in the Standard regime, we ran ablations by selectively restoring privileged information. This revealed a striking pattern:
- Providing only **object pose** improved success by just +4.4 points.
- Providing only **part geometry** improved success by +13.3 points.
- Providing **both pose and geometry** caused success to surge by +35.6 points, jumping from 24.4% to 60.0%.
Pose and geometry act multiplicatively rather than additively. Escaping a spatial constraint requires knowing not just where a part is, but the exact contours of the opening it must pass through.

### 5.2 How agents solved puzzles in the Privileged regime
Looking at successful runs in the Privileged regime, 64% relied on coding state-dependent waypoints with micro-adjustments, and 31% used motion planners (such as RRTs) written by the agents themselves. Agents constructed custom planners directly from privileged geometric data, finding solutions within a median of just 7 reset attempts.

### 5.3 Failure mode taxonomy and agent tendencies
Analyzing 2,214 failed runs revealed clear behavioral patterns:
- **Early stalls**: Only 7% of failed runs progressed past the halfway mark of a task. In the Standard regime, 53% of failures became permanently stuck on a single step.
- **Dominated by planning and execution errors**: Failures were driven mainly by planning errors (unreachable targets or collisions, 25%) and execution errors (grasp slips, 38%), while pure perception errors accounted for only 5%.
- **Good position, poor bounds**: Median object position error was just 1.5 mm. However, the median error on bounding box extents was 13.9 mm, showing agents struggled to infer object dimensions from vision alone.
- **Top performers act first**: Astra, Sol, and Opus spent only 32% to 42% of their efforts on extensive upfront planning, favoring an iterative trial-and-error approach that adjusted based on execution feedback.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: RoboARC highlights both the impressive reasoning capabilities and current blind spots of frontier agents under geometric constraints. The path forward points toward unifying high-level coding agents with closed-loop sensorimotor policies.
sections.details:
This study introduced RoboARC, a robotics benchmark centered on physical puzzles governed by tight spatial constraints.

The experiments demonstrate that frontier coding agents already possess the reasoning ability to autonomously write motion planners and clear complex puzzles, provided they know the shapes and poses of the parts. However, when forced to rely entirely on their own sensors in a single attempt, success rates drop by more than half. Meanwhile, current zero-shot VLA policies fail on these puzzles entirely.

Coding agents excel at global geometric reasoning but stumble during contact-heavy execution. Conversely, VLA models can make contact with objects but fail to reason through constraint pathways. The authors conclude that pairing a reasoning agent for global path planning with a closed-loop sensorimotor policy for contact feedback represents a compelling approach to overcoming spatial constraints.

sections.heading: Appendix: Task diversity and physics audits
sections.summary: The appendix provides details on the 90 task variations, domain randomization techniques, and physics auditing procedures used to verify penetration depths.
sections.details:
### Diverse task library
The suite encompasses diverse challenges: interlocked mechanical puzzles (e.g., interlocked claws, cast keyhole), extracting a sphere from a maze-like cage (hedgehog in cage), 3D buzz wire navigation, padlock unlocking, IKEA furniture assembly with bolts, and untying or threading flexible ropes.

### Domain randomization and determinism
Every task includes three distinct seeds that randomize room lighting, table materials (wood, metal, stone), object colors, and cloth textures. By masking SIMD instruction sets across CPU architectures, the MuJoCo simulation ensures bit-identical deterministic replays with matching state hashes across AMD and Intel hardware.

### Physics auditing (checking for pass-throughs)
All simulated solutions underwent contact-depth audits. Across 250 successful replays, the median penetration depth was 0.29 mm, closely matching the 0.22 mm median seen in reference solutions. This confirms that solutions were valid and did not exploit physics engine tunneling bugs.

takeaways: Manipulation difficulty stems not just from long task horizons, but from the narrowness of viable motion tubes under geometric constraints, requiring dedicated benchmarks.

When provided with exact part geometry and pose, modern LLM agents can write their own motion planners to solve 86% of puzzles, but inferring shapes and executing contacts from real sensors remains a major hurdle.
Object pose and part geometry yield small improvements alone, but combining both produces a massive synergy that drives success rates from 24% to 60%.
A hybrid setup combining high-level geometric reasoning agents with low-level closed-loop sensorimotor (VLA) policies offers a promising path forward.
limitations: Some rigid-body tasks use assisted grasping, bypassing one of the most challenging real-world hurdles: establishing a stable physical grasp.
Evaluations are primarily conducted in the MuJoCo simulator, with real-world validation limited to a single buzz wire task.
Evaluation costs are exceptionally high, consuming large volumes of API tokens and up to three hours of inference time per task.
